elements.text: One of the most costly aspects initially was the bitcoind "unspendable" distinction (arbitrary, basically just script too long and first opcode is op_return), required hitting the output table body for every single output during the scan. I was able to bypass that entirely by setting that bit into the outs association table when each output is written (essentially free), and was able to merge this bit into an existing oversized link (still > 10 years of run time) to avoid any store size increase. We have a far more expansive concept of unspendable which is set during script parse, allowing script validation to be bypassed. But that's not cached and wouldn't help here anyway. IOW, there are a lot of provably unspendable scripts that are considered unspent (spendable) by Core, and those get counted in this accounting.

elements.text: I'm out of release preview punch list items, apart from unit test expansion (which is ongoing). So I've taken on two items on the v4 release list.
Generalize addressing for bip155 support and implement Tor, I2P and cjdns addressing.
Implement outbound connection binding, and load balance outbound connections.

I've decided against support for network bridging, so Tor, I2p, and IP will apply to the full node, not on a per-channel basis. Not only is this dramatically simpler, it also forecloses a Core privacy leak. Obviously the networks need to be bridged, but this is not the way to do it. A bridge is simply two nodes on distinct networks sharing a private manual IP connection.

elements.text: In reviewing the bitcoind endpoints I found that Core has a "feature" that allows the node to be configured to stop providing blocks once the byte upload has exceeded a threshold in a 24hr period. It drops peers that make block requests after this limit is reached. The node keeps advertising NODE_NETWORK, which makes this a bug. We implement DoS protection via a continuously imposed rate limit on outbound traffic. We throttle the next request reader based on the previous response size, so as to not exceed the outbound rate (except instantaneously). Since we also manage peer count, the combination allows the admin to set an overall rate limit. This prevents one channel from eating the bandwidth limit for all others.

elements.text:
There is quite a bit of new functionality driven from the network management method implementations. For example, there has been no way to enumerate running channels, as that starts breaking the lock-free network design. When Core audits the channel set for diagnostics, it takes a lock of the entire network - all channels. We send a message to all channel subscribers and they write a response, and we collect the responses when they are all handled, or collect the first responder as the case may be.

So I generalized this approach to enumerate channels, to get their state and statistics, etc. I also added a broadcast to stop a channel, including the option to stop and drop a manual channel from retry. These are targetable by unresolved and resolved (for non-proxied IP addresses) address. I also added per-channel-per-p2p-message-type send and receive byte counters, and total send/receive byte counters for the process lifetime. These then report back to the caller and summarize as necessary once collected.

In order to avoid contention on lots of channels updated lots of atomics to obtain the process totals, I implemented a mechanism whereby the process totals are only updated when a channel stops, running channel totals are swept dynamically, and the two are reconciled by the caller to get the running totals. This is guarded by the set of running channel IDs being maintained at the point of channel drop, atomically with the total update. So the sweep can be subtracted from totals if double-counted. So a consistent snapshot in time with no locking, and the collection cost moved to the administrative caller.

elements.text:
I've closed one of the two remaining open DoS protection features.

We pace all responses to their requests, and treat jrpc batched requests as individual cycles, reading only one at a time, making it inherently impossible to DoS the node by request flooding. One request, response completed, next request. We also gate the query of a next item on the completed send of its predecessor (e.g. block requests), flattening the peak cost of any single request down to its individual parts - even if those parts are a single logical message response. The caller is forced to read each portion before we query the next.

However, with full duplex we can send notifications, which are "responses" without a corresponding request. Even though we control the size of each response, we can't control the rate at which they are read. So notifications can backlog indefinitely, just du to slow reading. Some notifications can be dropped, but in the supported interfaces this really only applies to the bitcoind zeromq interface, since zmq adds a sequence identifier to broadcasts, allowing messages to be dropped when the high water mark (HWM) is reached. For others, correctness dictates that the channel must be dropped.

This implies some rational measure of backlog, which isn't always as straightforward as it may seem. For performance reasons we don't serialize objects to a buffer in order to send them. Sometimes the serialization happens directly from the source to the socket, as chunks are read by the recipient. And the backlogged closures have their own cost, which can be more than the message itself. But all backlog now includes size approximations sufficient for the DoS guard. So while a full-duplex channel is at its HWN it either starts dropping messages (zeromq) or it drops the channel (p2p, tcp-jrpc, ws).

Found some open issues in the P2P implementation here, so ended up fully generalizing the design pattern across all channel types. Client-server interfaces have a pretty clear request-response vs. event-notify pattern, and r/r is guarded by not reading the next off the socket until the previous is fully sent. The e/n patter requires cost accounting, as otherwise a slow counterparty can force buffer overflow.

On p2p there wasn't a clear distinction between r/r and e/n, so I created one, which is controlled by the protocol invoking notify(message) (vs send(message)) in the cases where the message originates from an event, not a request. P2P is more complex than client/server given that multiple protocols may subscribe to and handle the same request on a given channel. This is because p2p mixes inventory types (e.g. tx and block) in one message, and similar issues, which makes it harder to isolate protocol behavior. So the request is only complete after all subscribers have released the message.

So both the notification distinction and the concurrent handling are now generalized to p2p, which closes the DoS gap there. This also coincides with the low level network code subsuming the monitor() function into this framework. A monitor is created on a channel when the message handler leaves the strand (e.g. to do potentially parallel and long-running tasks). This arms the socket to monitor for a counterparty drop, which then propagates cancellation. So this is now automatic in the r/r cycle. When a method departs the strand it explicitly requests a handle, which arms the monitor, and is automatically disarmed when the handle destructs.

So overall less code, simpler to get right, even less to manage in the protocol, correct/consistent across interfaces, and flexible enough to handle complex scenarios.
